questions.q: What is the single biggest risk with manual lineage documentation, according to this lesson?
options: It decays the moment the real pipeline changes and nobody remembers to update the document
It is illegal to write lineage down by hand in most industries
It requires expensive specialized hardware
It can only be used by people with a programming background
questions.explain: Manual documentation is cheap to start but has no mechanism to stay in sync with a changing pipeline, so it silently goes stale.

questions.q: How does static parsing derive lineage, per this lesson?
options: By reading the actual source code — SQL, ETL job definitions, transformation configs — without running it
By asking end users to fill out a survey about the data
By measuring network traffic between servers
By randomly sampling rows from a table
questions.explain: Static parsing is a code-analysis approach: a tool reads what the code says it does and derives lineage from that, without executing it.

questions.q: What makes runtime capture potentially the most trustworthy of the three approaches, according to the lesson?
options: It captures the real, executed behavior of a pipeline rather than an inference about intended behavior
It is the cheapest of the three approaches to set up
It never requires any instrumentation of running systems
It can see jobs that have never actually executed
questions.explain: Runtime capture observes what actually happened when a pipeline ran, rather than inferring intent from code or relying on a human's memory — but it does require instrumentation and only sees executed jobs.

questions.q: What problem do open lineage standards like OpenLineage address, per this lesson?
options: That lineage recorded in each tool's own proprietary format can't be combined into one coherent picture across tools
That data pipelines run too slowly without a standard in place
That manual lineage documentation is too expensive to ever justify
That lineage standards eliminate the need for any lineage capture at all
questions.explain: A common structured format lets lineage emitted by different tools in a pipeline be stitched together into one shared graph, rather than staying isolated in each tool's own format.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what pattern do most real organizations actually follow for capturing lineage?
options: They mix automated capture for technical detail, manual documentation for legacy gaps, and a human-maintained business-lineage layer on top
They rely exclusively on manual documentation for every system
They rely exclusively on runtime capture and never use static parsing
They avoid lineage standards entirely to keep systems simple
questions.explain: The lesson describes a common real-world pattern of combining automated technical capture, manual documentation for gaps automation can't reach, and a people-maintained business-readable layer.
